name: Oughtred sliding scales
summary: William Oughtred slid two logarithmic scales against each other instead of using dividers, the arrangement that became the slide rule.
description: Two Gunter-type logarithmic scales moved alongside one another so their relative displacement replaces transfer with dividers.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.

date.label: 1620s
date.basis: Whipple dates the attributed sliding-scale invention only to the 1620s; the anchor is a display midpoint, not a documented year.

events.statement: Two Gunter-type logarithmic scales moved alongside one another so their relative displacement replaces transfer with dividers.
events.caveats: Approximate retrospective attribution; this node does not equate an early conception, a 1632 description, and a surviving instrument.

evidence.locator: Section The true way of Art, first paragraph
evidence.supports: Attributes juxtaposed moving Gunter scales to Oughtred in the 1620s, with cautious wording.

events.statement: An English printed volume offered for sale described Oughtred’s two rulers for calculation.
events.caveats: A manual’s public availability does not establish that an instrument had been sold, delivered, or actually used by every reader.

evidence.supports: Identifies the two rulers and the book’s public sale.

links.statement: Oughtred put two Gunter-type scales alongside one another and moved them relatively, dispensing with separate dividers.
links.alternatives: Dividers continued to operate a single scale; circular arrangements offered another geometry.
links.caveats: Approximate attribution and date; no automatic 1622 precision is added.
links.timing: The receiving decade overlaps the source year, but the historical statement explicitly describes adaptation of already existing Gunter scales.
